title: The morning offering
hookLine: offering the whole day, its work and joys and troubles
tomorrow: why did a hungry man climb onto a roof at midday?

lines: A PACKAGE WITH NO PACKING SLIP.
BUT HOW SHOULD IT BE SAID?
cards: A day arrives like a package with no packing slip. A test, an email, maybe a laugh, maybe bad news, none of it opened yet. Some Christians give the whole box away before it's opened.
They call it a morning offering: the day's work, joys and troubles, handed to God at the start. And Christians disagree, kindly, about how it should be said.

teach.b: The idea comes from Paul, writing to the Romans: “present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service.” Bodies: the whole person who'll walk through the day.
A sacrifice that stays alive and goes to work. Now the two views. One side says: use words the church has prayed before you.
Catholics have a prayer called the Morning Offering, which offers to Jesus the day's prayers, works, joys and sufferings.
Thomas Ken, an English bishop, wrote a morning hymn asking God to direct all he plans, does or says that day.

teach.h: SET WORDS: AFTER THIS MANNER PRAY.
teach.b: Their best case: Jesus gave his followers set words himself, “After this manner therefore pray ye,” and the Psalms are a book of set prayers. Set words carry you on mornings when your own have gone.
The other side says: speak plainly, in your own words.

Their best case comes from the same chapter of Matthew, a few lines earlier: “use not vain repetitions.” Words you mean, they say, over words you recite. One to tell a friend: both sides quote Jesus in Matthew six.
And both agree on what goes in: all of it.

teach.h: MY TIMES ARE IN THY HAND.
teach.b: A psalm says, “My times are in thy hand.”
Times, plural, the good hour and the hard one. Some Christians keep both: a set line on rushed mornings, their own words on slow ones.

how: Some Catholics pray the Morning Offering on waking; other Christians offer the day to God in a morning hymn, a set prayer or their own words.

o: a hymn a choir sings at dawn on feast days
a gift of money collected at a sunrise service
handing the whole day to God as it begins

games.q: two ways to offer a morning — tap the pairs.
p: present your bodies a living sacrifice
the case for your own words

s: a morning offering hands over only the day's work
it offers the joys and the troubles too: all of it.
the case for set prayers and the case for your own words both quote Matthew 6
after this manner pray ye, and use not vain repetitions, a few lines apart.

games.q: you pray in your own words. your friend reads the same printed morning prayer every day. state her side at its strongest.
o: Jesus gave set words himself, and they carry you when your own run out.
set words are more official, so God hears them more clearly.
printed prayers are for people who haven't learned to pray yet.
games.why: the set-words side leans on after this manner pray ye and the Psalms. the own-words side leans on use not vain repetitions. both offer the whole day.

practice: Say out loud, at speaking volume, three things today holds: one task, one thing you're looking forward to, one thing you dread.
If you pray, hand all three over, in set words you know or in your own; if not, simply let none of the three be left off the list.

orig.note: Paul's Greek in Romans 12:1: a living sacrifice.

carryVoice: Your line: all of it. Set words or your own, the offering leaves nothing out. Day 1683, offered.
